title: Storage has one promise: the bytes you write come back
body:
Storage has one promise that outranks everything else: when you write data, you can later read the same bytes back. Speed, cost, and features are secondary. A slow photo service annoys users; a service that loses photos loses them forever.

The surprising lesson of this chapter is that disks dying is the easy problem. The hard problems are silent corruption, software bugs, and humans or tools deleting the wrong thing. Those, not random hardware failure, cause almost all real data loss.
deeper:
The chapter uses a running example: a global app with 1 billion users. It stores profiles, photos and videos, messages, logs, and an analytics lake. Each of these needs a different answer to the question of how safe is safe enough. Profiles are small and critical because users need them to log in. Messages are write-heavy. Photos and videos are huge blobs. Logs can often be re-derived. Analytics users can wait hours.

The chapter's arc follows how data really gets lost. It starts with durability math for hardware failure, then shows why that math is optimistic: failures are correlated, bytes change silently, CPUs miscompute, software bugs hit the whole fleet at once, and operators or tools delete the wrong thing. It then covers the defenses: checksums and scrubbing, formal methods, backups that are separate from replication, disaster recovery strategies, DR testing, and blast-radius reduction with cells and shuffle sharding. It closes with real public postmortems, and notes that none of them was caused by too many disks failing at random.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter call disk failure the easy problem?
quiz.a: Disk failure is loud: the system notices and repairs automatically. Silent corruption, software bugs, and wrong deletes go unnoticed or get replicated everywhere, so they cause almost all real losses.

title: Durable, available, reliable: three different promises
body:
Three words get mixed up. Durability means the data still exists and is correct, even if you cannot reach it right now. Availability means you can read or write the data right now. Reliability is the broad property that the system does what it promises over time; it includes both.

The distinction matters because they can fail separately and cost different amounts. A system can be unreachable yet lose nothing, or be fully reachable while quietly handing back wrong bytes.
deeper:
The 2017 Amazon S3 outage in us-east-1 is the classic example of durable but not available: objects could not be read for hours, yet no data was lost. Users were cut off, but the bytes survived and came back intact once the index and placement subsystems restarted.

The opposite failure is sneakier. A system can be available and quietly return wrong bytes. That is a durability failure hiding behind a healthy dashboard: every health check passes, requests succeed with low latency, and yet the data served is corrupt. Monitoring built around availability (error rates, latency) will not catch it at all. You need integrity checks such as end-to-end checksums to see it.

The practical takeaway from the key takeaways: durability and availability are different goals with different costs, so ask for both explicitly. When a product owner says the data must be safe, clarify whether they mean it must never be lost, or must always be reachable, or both, because the designs and budgets differ.

quiz.q: How can a storage system be fully available and still have a durability failure?
quiz.a: It can serve requests successfully while returning silently corrupted bytes. The dashboard looks healthy, but the data is no longer correct, so it has effectively been lost.

title: AFR and MTTF: two ways to say how often drives die
body:
The basic input to durability math is the annualized failure rate (AFR): the fraction of drives that fail in one year. Vendors also quote MTTF, mean time to failure, often 1 to 2.5 million hours.

The two are linked: AFR is roughly 8,760 hours (one year) divided by MTTF. So an MTTF of 1 million hours means an AFR of about 0.88%. AFR is the more useful number for planning, because it directly tells you how many drives to expect to replace each year.
deeper:
The catch is where the numbers come from. Vendor MTTF figures come from lab tests, and real fleets are messier: drives run at different temperatures, workloads, and ages, and some models or manufacturing batches are simply worse than others. A datasheet MTTF of 2.5 million hours would imply an AFR well under 1%, but real fleets typically see higher.

The best public data comes from Backblaze, a cloud backup and storage company that has published statistics on its own drive fleet every quarter since 2013. Its numbers show real-world AFR around 1 to 2% per year, and show that failure rates vary by drive model and by age.

The conversion is worth memorizing because it lets you sanity-check any claim quickly: divide 8,760 by the MTTF in hours to get an approximate yearly failure fraction. If someone quotes MTTF and plans capacity from it, convert it and compare against fleet data before trusting it. Planning from the datasheet leads to underestimating repair load and spare capacity.

quiz.q: Why should you plan with fleet AFR rather than vendor MTTF?
quiz.a: Vendor MTTF comes from lab tests; real fleets see higher and more varied failure rates by model, batch, and age. Fleet data like Backblaze's reflects what you will actually replace.

title: Backblaze: 344,196 drives say real AFR is about 1.4%
body:
Backblaze publishes failure statistics for its own drive fleet every quarter since 2013. It reported an overall AFR of 1.36% for 2025, across 344,196 hard drives and 30 drive models. The figure was 1.55% for 2024 (recomputed) and 1.70% for 2023.

Averages hide variation: some individual models failed much more often than average, and failure rates change with drive age. The lesson is to plan with real fleet numbers, not the datasheet, and to expect some drive models to be bad batches.
deeper:
Why this data is so valuable: the chapter calls it the best public data on how drives actually behave in a real fleet, as opposed to vendor lab tests. The chapter uses the 2025 average, 1.36% per year, as the lambda in its own back-of-envelope durability calculation.

Two cautions follow from the variation. First, a bad batch is a correlated risk: if all three replicas of an object happen to sit on drives from the same flawed model or batch, their failures are not independent, and the neat durability math breaks. This is one reason to spread copies across failure domains and, ideally, across drive models. Second, age matters, so a fleet's AFR drifts as drives get older, and the repair system must handle rising failure rates without human help.

The key takeaways summarize it: real drive failure rates are around 1 to 2% per year, and at scale several drives fail every day, so repair must be automatic.

quiz.q: Why is a bad batch of drives dangerous beyond just raising the average AFR?
quiz.a: Drives from the same batch tend to fail together, so replicas on them fail in a correlated way, breaking the independent-failure assumption behind durability math.

title: At scale, drive failure is background noise, not an event
body:
With an AFR of about 1.4%, a fleet of 100,000 drives should expect about 1,400 drive failures a year, roughly 4 per day. Companies with millions of drives see far more.

At that scale, drive failure is not an incident. It is a constant background process, like garbage collection. The system must detect failed drives and heal itself, re-creating lost copies automatically, without humans in the loop. Any design that pages an engineer per dead disk will not survive growth.
deeper:
The arithmetic is simple: failures per year equals fleet size times AFR. 100,000 drives times 0.014 is 1,400; divide by 365 and you get about 4 per day. Multiply the fleet by ten and you have about 40 per day, every day, including weekends and holidays.

This framing changes how you design. Repair is not a runbook; it is a core subsystem with its own capacity budget. It needs spare disk space to re-create copies into, network bandwidth reserved so repair does not starve user traffic (or vice versa), and automation to decide where new copies go while respecting failure domains.

It also connects directly to durability. As the next ideas show, data is only at risk while a copy is missing, so how fast the automatic repair runs sets the durability of the whole system. A manual process that takes a day to notice and replace a drive leaves data exposed for that entire day, four times a day, across the fleet. Automatic, fast healing is both an operational necessity and the main durability lever.

quiz.q: For a fleet of 100,000 drives at 1.4% AFR, why must repair be fully automated?
quiz.a: About 1,400 drives fail a year, roughly 4 a day. Humans cannot keep up, and slow manual repair leaves data exposed longer, lowering durability.

title: You only lose data when failures overlap in the repair window
body:
With three replicas on three different drives, you lose data only if all three drives fail before you finish making a new copy. The time to make that new copy is the repair time, also called MTTR (mean time to repair).

This gives the most important intuition in the chapter: you are only vulnerable during the repair window. Make the window small, and overlapping failures become very rare. Durability is less about how often drives fail and more about how quickly you replace what was lost.
deeper:
Think of it as a race. When the first drive fails, the clock starts. If a second and then third drive holding the same data fail before repair completes, the data is gone. If repair wins, you are back to three healthy copies and the race resets.

That is why durability engineering focuses so heavily on repair: detection speed (how fast you notice the drive is dead), prioritization (repair the data that has lost the most copies first), and throughput (how quickly the missing bytes can be re-created elsewhere).

The window also explains why larger drives are a durability concern, not just a capacity one. A bigger drive holds more data, so rebuilding it takes longer if you copy it from a single source, and the exposure window stretches from hours to more than a day. The fix, covered in later cards, is to scatter data in small chunks across many drives so that repair is parallel and the window shrinks to minutes.

Note the model assumes failures are independent. Correlated events such as power loss or firmware bugs can take out several copies at once, skipping the race entirely.

quiz.q: Why does the repair window matter more than the raw failure rate for three-replica durability?
quiz.a: Loss needs all copies to fail before repair finishes. Shrinking the window makes overlapping failures rare, which cuts loss probability sharply even at the same failure rate.

title: Back-of-envelope: loss probability is about 6 x AFR^3 x T^2
body:
Assume three replicas on independent drives, AFR per drive lambda = 0.0136 per year, and repair time T. Loss needs a chain: one of 3 drives fails (rate 3 lambda per year), then one of the other 2 fails before repair (probability about 2 lambda T), then the last fails before repair (about lambda T).

Multiply them: the yearly probability of losing a given piece of data is about 6 x lambda cubed x T squared. Always label assumptions like these, because they drive the answer.
deeper:
Plugging in numbers. With T = 1 day (1/365 year), lambda T is 3.7 x 10^-5 and the yearly loss probability per object is about 1.1 x 10^-10, roughly 10 nines. With T = 1 hour (1/8,760 year), lambda T is 1.6 x 10^-6 and the loss probability is about 2 x 10^-13, roughly 12 to 13 nines.

The assumptions are stated explicitly: the Backblaze 2025 average AFR, three replicas on three independent drives, independent failures, and a fixed repair time. The chapter flags independence as a big and unrealistic assumption. Real failures are correlated through batches, power events, firmware, and software bugs, so the true risk is higher than this model says.

The value of the calculation is not the exact number. It is the shape of the formula: loss probability grows with the cube of the failure rate and the square of the repair time. That tells you which knobs matter. You cannot do much about lambda beyond buying better drives, but T is under your control through software, placement, and bandwidth.

quiz.q: In the formula 6 x lambda^3 x T^2, why does T appear squared?
quiz.a: After the first failure, two more drives must each fail inside the repair window. Each has probability proportional to T, so together they scale with T squared.

title: Cut repair time 24x, cut loss risk about 576x
body:
Moving repair time from 1 day to 1 hour is a 24x reduction. Because three-replica loss probability scales with T squared, that cut the loss probability by about 576x (24 squared), from about 10 nines to about 12 to 13 nines.

The general rule: with n replicas, loss probability scales with T to the power (n minus 1), because after the first failure, n minus 1 more failures must all land inside the repair window. Faster repair pays off more the more replicas you have.
deeper:
This scaling law is a quick mental tool. The chapter's check-your-understanding example: cut repair time from 12 hours to 3 hours, a 4x reduction, and with three replicas the annual loss probability drops about 16x, because two more failures must both happen inside the now shorter window.

With four replicas the exponent is 3, so the same 4x faster repair gives about 64x improvement. With two replicas the exponent is 1, and faster repair gives only a proportional gain.

The key takeaways phrase the consequence directly: with three copies, loss probability scales with repair time squared, so fast, parallel, declustered repair is the cheapest durability win. It is cheap because repair speed is mostly a software and network problem, using bandwidth you already own, rather than a hardware purchase that adds cost to every byte forever.

The caveat, again, is that this all assumes independent failures. The squared benefit does nothing against a correlated event that wipes several copies at the same moment.

quiz.q: With three replicas, repair time drops from 12 hours to 3 hours. Roughly how does annual loss probability change, and why?
quiz.a: About 16x lower. Loss scales with T squared for three replicas, since two more failures must both occur inside the 4x shorter window.

title: Why faster repair beats a fourth replica: the cost argument
body:
A fourth replica improves durability math a lot, so why do storage engineers say faster repair matters more? The first reason is cost.

A fourth replica costs 33% more disk, forever, for every byte you store. At large scale that is an enormous recurring bill. Faster repair, by contrast, is mostly software and network bandwidth that you already own. Shrinking the repair window buys a large durability gain (24x faster repair gives about 576x lower loss risk) without buying a single extra drive.
deeper:
Going from three to four replicas changes the exponent on T from 2 to 3, which is powerful. But it multiplies raw storage by 4/3 across the entire fleet. For a system storing exabytes, that is a vast purchase of disks, racks, power, and floor space, and the cost never goes away because every new byte also needs the extra copy.

Repair speed improvements are closer to one-time engineering: better failure detection, prioritizing the most endangered data, spreading data so many drives participate in repair, and reserving enough network bandwidth for repair traffic. Once built, they improve durability for all existing and future data at little marginal cost.

The other two reasons, covered in the next cards, are that drives keep getting bigger (making whole-disk rebuilds dangerously slow) and that parallel, declustered repair fixes this. Together they explain why systems like GFS, Colossus, Tectonic, and S3 invest in chunking and scattering data rather than simply adding more copies. Erasure coding follows the same philosophy: get durability through smart placement and repair rather than brute-force replication.

quiz.q: Why is adding a fourth replica usually a worse durability investment than faster repair?
quiz.a: The fourth replica adds 33% more disk for every byte forever, while faster repair mostly uses software and network bandwidth you already own, giving large gains cheaply.

title: A 24 TB drive rebuilt from one disk: 33 hours exposed
body:
Drives keep getting bigger, and that stretches repair windows. Rebuilding a 24 TB drive from a single source disk at 200 MB/s takes 24 x 10^12 / 2 x 10^8 = 120,000 seconds, about 33 hours.

For those 33 hours, the data that lived on the failed drive has one fewer copy and is exposed to further failures. Bigger drives make repair windows longer unless you change the design, which is why whole-disk mirroring becomes more dangerous as capacities grow.
deeper:
The problem is that one disk's bandwidth caps the rebuild. With whole-disk mirroring, the replacement is filled from one surviving mirror, so repair time is simply capacity divided by single-disk throughput. Capacity has grown much faster than per-disk bandwidth, so rebuild time keeps growing.

Compare with older, smaller drives. The chapter's quiz contrasts 24 TB drives with 2 TB drives: a 2 TB rebuild at the same speed would take under 3 hours, while 24 TB takes over a day. Since loss probability scales with T squared for three replicas, a 12x longer window means roughly 144x higher loss risk for the same design.

In practice, a rebuild also competes with user traffic, so the 200 MB/s figure may be optimistic during busy periods, making the real window longer still. And the longer a rebuild runs, the more chance of a correlated event, such as a second drive from the same batch failing under the extra rebuild load. The design answer is not to buy faster disks but to change placement so that many disks share the repair work.

quiz.q: Why does a fleet of 24 TB drives make whole-disk mirroring more dangerous than 2 TB drives did?
quiz.a: Rebuild from one source is limited by one disk's bandwidth, so 24 TB takes over a day, leaving data exposed that whole time. Longer windows sharply raise overlap risk.

title: Declustered repair: 1,000 drives rebuild 24 TB in 20 minutes
body:
Parallel repair fixes the big-drive problem. If a lost drive's data is spread in small chunks across 1,000 other drives, each surviving drive only re-copies a small piece. Even at just 20 MB/s per drive, 1,000 drives rebuild 24 TB in about 1,200 seconds, roughly 20 minutes instead of 33 hours.

This is called declustered or distributed repair. It is why systems like GFS, Colossus, Tectonic, and S3 split data into chunks and scatter them widely instead of mirroring whole disks.
deeper:
The chapter's diagram contrasts the two paths after a drive fails. Whole-disk mirror: one source disk copies 24 TB, about 33 hours exposed, higher chance of overlapping failure. Chunks scattered on 1,000 disks: each copies a small piece, about 20 minutes exposed, much lower chance of overlapping failure.

Note the per-drive rate is deliberately low. At 20 MB/s, each drive gives up only a fraction of its bandwidth to repair, so user traffic is barely affected, yet aggregate repair throughput is about 20 GB/s. The same aggregate speed also means that the new copies land on many different drives, avoiding a single hot spot.

The cost of declustering is metadata and placement complexity: the system must track where every chunk lives and ensure the replicas of any chunk sit in different failure domains. It also means any single drive failure touches data belonging to many objects, so repair must be well automated.

From the durability formula, moving T from 33 hours to 20 minutes is about a 100x shorter window, which for three replicas is roughly 10,000x lower loss probability.

quiz.q: How does scattering chunks across 1,000 drives shrink the repair window?
quiz.a: Each surviving drive re-copies only a small piece in parallel, so aggregate bandwidth is huge: 24 TB rebuilds in about 20 minutes instead of 33 hours from one source.

title: Erasure coding: 1.4x overhead, but repair must be engineered
body:
Erasure coding follows the same durability logic as replication. A 10+4 code splits data into 10 data fragments plus 4 parity fragments and survives any 4 lost fragments, at 1.4x storage overhead instead of the 3x of triple replication.

The catch is repair. Rebuilding a lost fragment requires reading from many other fragments, not just copying one replica. So repair speed and repair traffic must be engineered carefully, or the repair window grows and the durability benefit shrinks.
deeper:
Erasure coding was covered in earlier chapters of the book; here the point is how it fits the repair-window model. A 10+4 code can lose any 4 of its 14 fragments and still reconstruct the data, so loss requires five overlapping failures within the repair window, which is very rare if repair is fast and fragments live in independent failure domains.

The storage saving is large: 1.4x versus 3x means less than half the raw disk for the same logical data.

The trade-off is repair amplification. To rebuild one missing fragment, the system must read enough surviving fragments to reconstruct it, which means much more network and disk traffic per repaired byte than simple copying from a replica. If that traffic is not budgeted and spread out, repair either runs slowly (lengthening exposure) or floods the network (hurting user traffic). So the same principles apply: scatter fragments widely, repair in parallel, and prioritize stripes that have lost the most fragments.

quiz.q: Why does erasure coding need more careful repair engineering than replication?
quiz.a: Rebuilding a fragment reads from many other fragments, creating much more repair traffic. Without careful budgeting, repair is slow, lengthening the exposure window, or floods the network.

title: What S3's '11 nines' actually promises
body:
Amazon S3 says Standard storage is designed for 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability of objects over a year. The S3 FAQ explains it this way: if you store 10,000,000 objects, you can on average expect to lose a single object once every 10,000 years.

Read carefully: it is a design target from a model, not a measured count. Nobody has run S3 for 10,000 years. The model mostly covers hardware failure, with independent-ish failures, repair times, and placement across failure domains.
deeper:
The figure comes from the same kind of reasoning as the chapter's back-of-envelope calculation, applied with S3's real redundancy scheme, repair speeds, and placement across failure domains. It is a statement about how the system is engineered to handle hardware faults, not an audited historical loss rate.

That is still meaningful: it tells you hardware failure is essentially a solved problem for this class of storage. But it is easy to misread as meaning your data cannot be lost. The number says nothing about the far more common ways data disappears, which are the subject of the next card.

The key takeaways put it plainly: 11 nines is a model-based design target for hardware failure. It does not cover deletes, bugs, account events, or correlated disasters, which cause almost all real losses. So when you see a durability figure like this, treat it as the floor of the problem solved for you, and plan your own protection, such as versioning, backups, and separate accounts, for everything above it.

quiz.q: Why can't the 11-nines figure be a measured statistic?
quiz.a: It predicts losing one of 10 million objects every 10,000 years; no one has operated S3 that long. It is a model-based design target for hardware failure.

title: 11 nines won't save you from your own DELETE
body:
The 11-nines durability model does not cover the ways data is most often lost: you deleting your own data, a bug in your application writing garbage, a compromised account, or a legal or billing event closing the account. It also does not cover large correlated disasters or provider control-plane mistakes.

These events are far more likely than 11-nines hardware events. A storage system with 11 nines of durability can therefore still lose your data, because the model's scope is much narrower than people assume.
deeper:
This is the answer to the chapter's first check-your-understanding question: why can a 99.999999999% durable system still lose your data? Because the target models hardware failures only. Customer or operator deletes, application bugs, account compromise, provider control-plane mistakes, and large correlated disasters sit outside the model, and they are far more likely.

From the storage system's point of view, a delete you issued is a successful operation, not a loss. Garbage written by your buggy app is stored with perfect durability. An attacker with your credentials is an authorized user. None of these register as failures, so no amount of redundancy helps; the redundant copies faithfully reflect the mistake.

The UniSuper incident of 2024 is a vivid example of the provider-side version: a blank parameter in an internal tool led to automatic deletion of a whole private cloud across two regions. The defenses for this category are different from the defenses for hardware: versioning, delayed or soft deletes, immutable backups, separate accounts and credentials, and copies held outside your primary provider's control plane.

quiz.q: Why does replication inside S3 not protect you from an accidental delete?
quiz.a: To S3, your delete is a valid operation, not a failure. The model covers hardware faults; the delete is applied to all copies, so you need versioning or separate backups.

title: Correlated failures break the independence math
body:
The independent-failure model behind nines calculations is optimistic. Real failures are correlated, meaning one cause takes out many copies at once.

Examples: drives from the same manufacturing batch fail together; a power event takes out a whole rack or building; a firmware bug affects every drive of a model; a software bug or bad deploy affects every server at once. When failures are correlated, several replicas can die simultaneously, skipping the repair-window race entirely and making the real risk much higher than the model predicts.
deeper:
The durability formula multiplies probabilities, which is only valid if one failure tells you nothing about another. Correlation destroys that. If three replicas share a rack and the rack loses power, the chance they all fail together is roughly the chance of the rack failing, not the cube of a single drive's failure rate.

Each correlated cause maps to a design response. Batch effects: spread copies across drive models and purchase batches. Power and building events: spread copies across racks, power zones, and buildings. Firmware bugs: stage firmware rollouts and avoid homogeneous fleets for critical data. Software bugs and bad deploys: deploy gradually, use cells, and keep backups that the buggy software cannot touch.

Software is the worst case. As Section 10.4 notes, a bug in crash recovery, caching, compaction, or garbage collection can lose or corrupt data across the whole fleet at once, breaking every independence assumption. That is why the chapter repeatedly says the hard problems are not random disk failures.

The patterns-across-incidents table makes the point empirically: no real incident in the chapter was too many disks failing at random.

quiz.q: Why does placing all three replicas in one rack undermine the durability calculation?
quiz.a: The replicas then share a fate: one power or rack event kills all three at once, so failures are correlated and the independent multiplication of probabilities no longer holds.

title: Google 2015: four lightning strikes, one correlated event
body:
In August 2015, four lightning strikes on the local power grid hit Google's europe-west1-b zone. Google reported that less than 0.000001% of Persistent Disk space in the zone was permanently lost, and about 5% of Standard Persistent Disks saw at least one I/O failure.

The loss was tiny, but it came from one correlated event, not from independent drive failures. Google's fixes included hardware that keeps cached data safe across power loss.
deeper:
The incident is a clean example of why independence assumptions fail. Nothing about individual drive reliability changed; a single external event hit many machines at the same instant. Any data whose protection depended on copies within the affected zone was exposed simultaneously.

The chapter's patterns table records it this way: root trigger, lightning; what turned it into a disaster, volatile cache during power loss; design fix, a persistent write path. In other words, some data was still sitting in volatile cache when power was lost, and that cached data vanished instead of reaching persistent storage.

The fix, making the write path persistent so cached data survives power loss, addresses the correlated failure directly. More replicas in the same zone would not have helped, because they would all have shared the same power event.

The broader lesson is that durability requires copies that do not share a fate. That leads to failure domains: placing replicas across disks, hosts, racks, power zones, and buildings.

quiz.q: In the 2015 lightning incident, why would adding more replicas within the same zone not have prevented the loss?
quiz.a: All replicas in the zone shared the same power event, so they would fail together. The fix was a persistent write path so acknowledged cached data survives power loss.

title: Failure domains: copies must not share a fate
body:
Real systems place replicas or erasure-coded fragments across failure domains: different disks, hosts, racks, power zones, and often different buildings (availability zones). A failure domain is a set of components that can fail together from a single cause.

The durability math only holds if the copies do not share a fate. Three replicas on three disks in one host are one host failure away from loss. Three replicas in three buildings survive a whole building going dark.
deeper:
Failure domains form a hierarchy. A disk can fail alone; a host failure takes all its disks; a rack failure takes all its hosts (top-of-rack switch or power); a power zone takes many racks; a building or availability zone takes everything inside it. Placement policy decides at which level copies must be separated.

Spreading wider costs something. Cross-building placement means writes travel farther and repair traffic crosses more expensive links. So systems choose the separation level based on how critical the data is and what latency the write path can tolerate.

The chapter extends the idea beyond physical infrastructure later. The UniSuper incident shows that a shared control plane, account, or contract is also a failure domain: its data sat in two geographic regions, but one provider-level deletion removed both. Multi-region is not independence if one control plane can delete every region at once. The same logic applies to shared software: a bug deployed everywhere at once is a failure domain spanning the whole fleet, which is why staged rollouts and cells matter.

quiz.q: Why doesn't having three replicas guarantee high durability by itself?
quiz.a: If the replicas share a failure domain, like one host, rack, or power zone, one event destroys them all. The math only holds when copies do not share a fate.

title: Three questions to ask whenever someone shows you 'N nines'
body:
Senior staff lens: when someone shows you N nines of durability, ask three questions. First, what failure model: independent or correlated failures? Second, what repair time is assumed, and is it measured at p99 during a busy day rather than on average when the system is idle? Third, what is outside the model: operator error, software bugs, deletes?

The honest answer to the third question usually matters more than the number itself, because that is where real data loss comes from.
deeper:
Each question targets a known weakness. The failure model question catches the independence assumption; a number computed with independent failures can overstate durability by orders of magnitude if copies share batches, racks, or software.

The repair time question matters because loss probability scales with T squared for three replicas. A design quoting a 1-hour repair that actually takes 10 hours at p99 when the network is busy is about 100x less durable than claimed. Measuring at p99 on a busy day, not the median on a quiet one, gives the realistic exposure window.

The out-of-model question is the most important. Operator error, tooling and configuration mistakes, and deletes triggered most of the chapter's case studies: the S3 typo, the GitLab wrong-server delete, the Azure config mistake, the UniSuper blank parameter. The rest (a DynamoDB network blip, a lightning strike at Google) were correlated events. None would show up in a nines calculation.

Using this lens in design reviews shifts the conversation from how many nines to what are we not protected against, which is where the real engineering work lies: backups, guardrails, and blast-radius limits.

quiz.q: Of the three questions about N nines, why does the out-of-model one usually matter most?
quiz.a: Operator error, software bugs, and deletes cause almost all real losses and are invisible to a hardware-failure model, so they dominate actual risk regardless of the headline number.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Silent corruption: when bytes change and nothing complains
body:
Losing a drive is loud: the system notices and repairs. Silent data corruption is worse. Bytes change and nothing reports an error. Reads succeed, dashboards stay green, and the data is simply wrong.

If you do not detect it, you will happily replicate the bad bytes, back them up, and serve them to users. Silent corruption turns every protection mechanism against you, because each one faithfully copies whatever it is given, so the damage spreads instead of being contained.
deeper:
The asymmetry between loud and silent failures is the core of this section. A dead drive triggers automatic repair within minutes. A flipped bit in a stored block triggers nothing until something reads the block and checks it, which for cold data may be years later.

Meanwhile, every system downstream treats the corrupt data as valid. Replication copies it to other nodes. Backups snapshot it, possibly overwriting older good backups as retention rotates. Migrations move it to new hardware. Caches serve it to users. By the time anyone notices, every copy may be bad.

This is why the chapter separates two kinds of protection. Replicas protect against loss, meaning a copy disappearing. Checksums and scrubbing protect against wrong bytes, meaning a copy that exists but is incorrect. A system needs both, and replication alone offers no defense against corruption.

The sources of silent corruption are more varied than most engineers expect: aging media, firmware bugs, memory bit flips, network errors that slip past TCP checksums, bugs in your own software, and even CPUs that compute wrong answers.

quiz.q: Why is silent corruption more dangerous than a drive failure?
quiz.a: A drive failure is detected and repaired. Silent corruption raises no error, so replication, backups, and caches spread the bad bytes until every copy may be wrong.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Where silent corruption comes from: disks, wires, code, CPUs
body: Silent corruption has many sources. Bit rot: magnetic or flash cells degrade over time; most errors are caught by the drive's own error-correcting code (ECC), but some are not. Misdirected or lost writes, where data lands in the wrong place or never lands, plus firmware bugs and memory bit flips. Network corruption: TCP checksums are only 16 bits, so rare corruptions slip through at scale. Software bugs in your own code. And CPUs that compute wrong answers.
deeper:
Each layer has some protection, but none is complete. Drive ECC catches the vast majority of media errors, yet at fleet scale the rare uncaught ones still happen regularly. A misdirected write is especially nasty: the drive reports success, the intended location keeps stale data, and another location is overwritten, so two blocks are wrong at once without any error.

The network point is about scale. A 16-bit checksum will fail to catch roughly one in 65,536 random corruptions. At the volume of traffic a large storage system moves, corrupted packets that happen to pass the TCP check are not hypothetical; they will occur. So relying on TCP for integrity is not enough.

Software bugs are the broadest source: serialization errors, off-by-one offsets, race conditions in caching or compaction. And the most surprising source, covered in its own cards, is defective CPUs that silently compute wrong results.

The common thread is that each layer only checks its own hop. The defense is to check integrity end to end, from the client that created the data to the client that reads it.

quiz.q: Why isn't TCP's checksum sufficient protection for data moving across a storage network?
quiz.a: TCP checksums are only 16 bits, so a small fraction of corruptions pass undetected. At storage scale, that fraction becomes real corrupted data, so end-to-end checksums are needed.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: End-to-end checksums: fingerprint early, verify late
body:
The fix for silent corruption is the end-to-end argument: check integrity at the ends, not only at each layer. A checksum (for example CRC32C, or a cryptographic hash like SHA-256) is a small fingerprint of the data.

The flow: the client computes a checksum when data is created; every layer stores and forwards it with the data; every read, copy, repair, and migration verifies it; and if a check fails, the system reads another replica and repairs the bad one.
deeper:
The key design principle is that the checksum is computed as early as possible and verified as late as possible. A checksum computed by the storage server after the data crossed a buggy network card protects nothing: it faithfully fingerprints the already-corrupted bytes, and every later check passes.

This is why the client, the original source of the data, should compute it. Then every hop in between, whether network, proxy, storage server, disk, repair process, or migration, is covered, because any change anywhere will cause a mismatch at the next verification.

Choosing the checksum is a trade-off. CRC32C is fast and has hardware support, making it good for detecting accidental corruption at high throughput. Cryptographic hashes like SHA-256 are slower but also resist deliberate tampering and have a vanishingly small collision chance.

Verification must happen on every movement of data, not just user reads. Repair and migration are exactly the moments when bad data might otherwise be copied onto fresh hardware and become the new source of truth. Combined with multiple replicas, a failed check becomes a self-healing event: read a good copy, rewrite the bad one.

quiz.q: Why is a checksum computed by the storage server less useful than one computed by the client?
quiz.a: If data was corrupted in transit before reaching the server, the server fingerprints the bad bytes and every later check passes. Client-side checksums cover every hop.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: S3, GFS, HDFS, Ceph, ZFS: checksums everywhere
body:
Real storage systems put checksums at every level. Amazon S3 lets clients send checksums with uploads (CRC32, CRC32C, SHA-1, SHA-256, and later CRC64NVME); S3 verifies them and stores them with the object.

GFS stored a checksum for every 64 KB block of each chunk, and chunkservers verified data before returning it. HDFS, Ceph (with its BlueStore backend), and ZFS all store per-block checksums. Integrity checking is a baseline feature of serious storage, not an optional extra.
deeper:
The S3 feature is a direct implementation of the end-to-end principle: the client computes the checksum before upload, S3 verifies it on arrival (catching network corruption), and stores it with the object. The range of supported algorithms lets clients trade speed (CRC variants) against tamper resistance (SHA variants).

GFS's per-64 KB-block design shows why granularity matters. Chunks in GFS were large, so a single checksum per chunk would mean rereading the whole chunk to verify any part of it, and a single bad bit would condemn the entire chunk. Per-block checksums let a chunkserver verify just the blocks being read and repair only the damaged block from another replica.

The chunkserver verifying before returning data is also important: it prevents a corrupt block from being served to a client or copied to another chunkserver during re-replication, which stops corruption from spreading.

HDFS, Ceph BlueStore, and ZFS follow the same per-block pattern, showing the idea spans distributed file systems, object stores, and local file systems.

quiz.q: Why did GFS checksum every 64 KB block rather than each whole chunk?
quiz.a: Per-block checksums let chunkservers verify only the blocks being read and repair just the damaged block, instead of rereading or discarding an entire large chunk.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Scrubbing: read everything on a schedule before it rots
body:
Checksums only help when someone reads the data. Cold data, such as old photos and old logs, may not be read for years. By then, two of three replicas might be silently bad.

Scrubbing is a background process that reads all data on a schedule, verifies checksums, and repairs bad copies from good ones. The trade-off is I/O cost: scrubbing competes with real traffic. Most systems throttle scrubbers and aim to cover all data every few weeks.
deeper:
Scrubbing turns detection from reactive to proactive. Without it, corruption in cold data accumulates silently. Each replica decays independently, and if nobody looks, eventually all copies of some object may be damaged, at which point repair is impossible. Scrubbing catches the first bad copy while good ones still exist and immediately repairs it, resetting the clock.

The schedule is a trade-off between risk and cost. Scrubbing every block means reading the entire dataset, which at large scale is an enormous amount of disk I/O. Run it too aggressively and it slows user requests; run it too rarely and more corruption accumulates between passes. Covering all data every few weeks is the common compromise, with throttling so the scrubber backs off when user traffic is high.

Scrubbing complements read-path verification: reads catch corruption in hot data quickly, and scrubbing ensures cold data is checked too. For the 1-billion-user example, old photos that nobody has viewed in years are exactly the data scrubbing exists to protect.

quiz.q: Why are checksums alone not enough to protect cold data?
quiz.a: Checksums only catch corruption when data is read. Cold data may go unread for years while several replicas rot; scrubbing reads it on a schedule and repairs early.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Common mistake: thinking replication protects against corruption
body:
A common mistake is treating replication as protection against corruption. It is not. If corruption is not detected, the replication system copies the bad data faithfully to every replica.

The two mechanisms solve different problems. Replicas protect against loss: a copy disappearing because a drive, host, or rack failed. Checksums and scrubbing protect against wrong bytes: a copy that still exists but is incorrect. A system needs both, and more replicas do nothing to catch corruption.
deeper:
Why the confusion happens: replication feels like safety, and it is, for the failure it targets. When a drive dies, the replica provides the data. But corruption is a different kind of failure. Nothing has disappeared; a copy is present and simply wrong, and the replication layer has no way of knowing which version is correct without integrity checks.

Worse, replication can actively spread corruption. If the primary's copy is corrupted before or during a write, the corrupt bytes are replicated. If a repair process copies from a silently corrupted replica to rebuild a lost one, the new copy is corrupt too. Without verification during repair, a system can replace good data with bad.

With checksums in place, replication becomes a corruption defense after all: a failed check identifies the bad copy, and the good replicas provide the source for repair. That is the combination the chapter recommends.

This mistake has a bigger sibling in Section 10.5: treating replication as a backup. Replication copies mistakes such as deletes and bad writes just as faithfully as it copies corrupted bytes.

quiz.q: Why doesn't adding more replicas protect you against silent corruption?
quiz.a: Undetected corruption gets copied faithfully to every replica. Replicas protect against loss; only checksums and scrubbing detect wrong bytes and identify which copy is good.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Meta 2021: CPUs that silently compute wrong answers
body:
For decades engineers assumed CPUs are correct: a faulty CPU crashes or reports a machine-check error. In 2021, papers from the two largest fleet operators showed this is false at scale.

Meta's paper, Silent Data Corruptions at Scale (Dixit et al., 2021), described CPUs with manufacturing defects that produce wrong results with no error signal. Monitoring hundreds of thousands of machines for over 18 months, Meta found hundreds of such defective CPUs. One computed a math function wrongly, causing files to go missing in a compressed database.
deeper:
The case study shows how a tiny compute error becomes data loss. A defective CPU returned a wrong result for a math function used in processing a compressed database. The wrong value was used in the logic handling file data, and files went missing. No crash, no error log, nothing flagged; the database was simply incomplete.

The scale detail matters: hundreds of defective CPUs among hundreds of thousands of machines. Rare per machine, but at fleet scale, guaranteed to be present at any given time. And because the corruption happens in computation, not storage, disk checksums may not help: if the CPU computes data wrongly before the checksum is taken, the checksum faithfully protects the wrong data.

Meta's conclusion was that fixing this requires three things together: hardware resilience (better manufacturing and testing), production detection (continuously testing machines in the fleet), and fault-tolerant software (designs that do not blindly trust a single computation). No single layer can solve it alone.

Google's parallel paper the same year, Cores that don't count, reached similar conclusions.

quiz.q: Why can't storage-layer checksums fully protect against a defective CPU?
quiz.a: If the CPU computes wrong data before the checksum is taken, or computes the checksum itself wrongly, the checksum matches corrupted data and every later check passes.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Google's 'mercurial cores' and the self-inverting AES bug
body:
Google's HotOS 2021 paper, Cores that don't count (Hochschild et al.), called silently faulty CPUs mercurial cores. Google observed on the order of a few mercurial cores per several thousand machines.

Symptoms included wrong answers from specific instructions, and a deterministic AES mis-computation that was self-inverting: encrypting and decrypting on the same core gave back the original data, so the bug was invisible until a different core tried to decrypt. A corrupted encryption key can make large amounts of data permanently unreadable.
deeper:
The self-inverting AES case shows why same-machine verification can be meaningless. The standard sanity check, encrypt then decrypt and compare, passed perfectly on the faulty core, because the core made the same error in both directions. The ciphertext written to storage was wrong in a way only a correct core would notice. Any other machine reading that data would fail to decrypt it, and if the plaintext had been deleted after the local check, the data would be gone.

The key corruption scenario is worse still. Encryption keys protect large volumes of data. If a mercurial core corrupts a key while generating or wrapping it, everything encrypted with that key may be permanently unreadable. One faulty computation, potentially millions of objects lost.

The frequency matters for planning: a few per several thousand machines means a large fleet always contains some. Defects can also appear with age and temperature, so a core that passed testing once may go bad later. That drives the defenses in the next card: repeated fleet screening, cross-machine verification, and quarantining suspect cores.

quiz.q: Why did the self-inverting AES bug escape an encrypt-then-decrypt check on the same core?
quiz.a: The faulty core made the same error both ways, so decrypting its own output returned the original. Only a different, correct core would fail to decrypt the stored ciphertext.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: Why bad CPUs threaten storage, and how fleets fight back
body:
Storage servers do a lot of computation: checksums, compression, encryption, and erasure codes. A bad core can produce a valid-looking checksum over wrong data, or corrupt an index that points to millions of objects.

Companies respond in three ways: screen the fleet repeatedly, since defects appear with age and temperature; verify on a different machine, for example decrypting on another core before deleting the plaintext; and quarantine suspect cores so they stop touching data.
deeper:
Each storage computation is a point where a mercurial core can inject corruption that downstream checks will not catch. Compression: wrong output that decompresses to wrong data. Encryption: ciphertext only the faulty core can read. Erasure coding: parity fragments that reconstruct garbage when later needed for repair. Checksums: a matching fingerprint over incorrect bytes.

Screening repeatedly, not just at purchase, is necessary because defects are not static. A CPU can pass acceptance testing and develop faults later as it ages or runs hot. Continuous production testing, running known computations and comparing to known answers, finds cores that have drifted.

Cross-machine verification is the direct fix for self-inverting bugs. Before deleting the plaintext after encrypting, decrypt on a different machine and confirm. Before trusting newly computed parity, verify elsewhere. The cost is extra compute, but it is applied at the critical points where a mistake would be irreversible.

Quarantine closes the loop: once a core is suspected, remove it from service rather than letting it keep producing subtly wrong results.

quiz.q: Why verify an encryption on a different machine before deleting the plaintext?
quiz.a: A mercurial core can produce ciphertext that it alone decrypts correctly. Verifying elsewhere confirms other machines can read it before the only good copy is deleted.

section: 10.3 Data corruption: when bytes change silently
title: The most dangerous corruption target: metadata and keys
body:
Senior staff lens: for a 1-billion-user app, the most dangerous place for silent corruption is not a single photo. It is metadata and keys: the index that maps photo IDs to storage locations, or the key that encrypts a million photos.

One corrupted photo affects one user. A corrupted index entry or key can make millions of objects unreachable or unreadable. Protect these with extra checks, multiple independent computations, and backups that are verified on different hardware.
deeper:
This is about blast radius per byte. Most bytes in a storage system are payload, and corruption there affects one object. A small number of bytes, such as index entries, placement maps, and encryption keys, have enormous leverage: they determine whether huge amounts of payload can be found or decrypted at all.

The chapter's check-your-understanding question illustrates it: a metadata server with a mercurial core that miscomputes CRC32C could produce checksums that match corrupted data, or corrupt an index affecting many objects. Defenses: client-computed end-to-end checksums verified on a different machine, repeated fleet screening and quarantine, and verified metadata backups.

In practice, extra protection for high-leverage data can mean computing it twice on different machines and comparing, keeping more copies than for payload, verifying backups by restoring them on independent hardware, and scrubbing it more often. The cost is small because metadata and keys are tiny compared with the payload they govern.

This theme recurs in the incidents: the DynamoDB 2015 outage and the S3 2017 outage both centered on metadata subsystems, showing metadata is often the real bottleneck and risk.

quiz.q: Why do metadata and encryption keys deserve more protection than ordinary photo bytes?
quiz.a: They have huge leverage: one corrupted index entry or key can make millions of objects unreachable or unreadable, while corrupting one photo affects just one object.

title: Software bugs, not hardware, are the biggest risk
body:
Hardware is not the biggest risk to stored data; software bugs are. A storage node runs crash recovery, concurrency control, caching, compaction, and garbage collection. A bug in any of them can lose or corrupt data across the whole fleet at once, because every server runs the same code.

That breaks every independence assumption in the durability math. And testing cannot cover every interleaving of concurrent operations and crashes, so large storage teams turn to formal methods: mathematically precise ways to specify and check behavior.
deeper:
Why software is so dangerous: hardware failures are mostly independent and local, so redundancy handles them. A software bug is identical on every machine. Deploy a flawed compaction routine and it can corrupt data on every node that compacts. Replicas do not help, because all replicas run the same buggy code.

The subsystems listed are exactly where subtle bugs hide. Crash recovery must reconstruct correct state from whatever partially written data survived a power loss. Concurrency means operations interleave in countless orders. Caching creates multiple copies of state that must agree. Compaction and garbage collection rewrite and delete data in the background, so a mistake permanently destroys data that looked unreferenced.

Testing struggles because the bugs depend on rare combinations: a specific interleaving of two writes, a crash at one exact instruction, a retry arriving during compaction. The number of possible orderings is astronomically large, and tests sample only a tiny fraction.

Formal methods address this by precisely defining correct behavior and using tools to explore many or all executions systematically. The chapter covers two AWS approaches: TLA+ for designs and lightweight formal methods for ShardStore's code.

quiz.q: Why does a software bug break the independence assumptions behind durability math?
quiz.a: Every server runs the same code, so one bug can lose or corrupt data on all replicas at once, a perfectly correlated failure that redundancy cannot absorb.

title: TLA+ at AWS: a model checker found a 35-step bug
body:
TLA+ is a language for writing a precise specification of a system's design: its states and the transitions allowed between them. A model checker then explores all possible executions of a small version of the system and reports any that violate the rules.

AWS engineers described in Communications of the ACM (Newcombe et al., 2015) how they had used TLA+ since 2011 on complex systems including S3 and DynamoDB. The model checker found subtle bugs that tests and reviews had missed.
deeper:
The standout example: one DynamoDB bug needed a sequence of 35 steps to appear. A trace that long is one humans would be very unlikely to find by reasoning or reviewing, and random tests would be unlikely to stumble into it. The model checker found it because it systematically explores every possible ordering in a small configuration.

The small-version trick is what makes this practical. Real systems have thousands of nodes and unbounded data, which no tool can fully explore. But many design bugs show up with just a few nodes and a few operations. Checking every execution of a tiny system catches them before code is written.

The limitation, which motivates the ShardStore work, is that TLA+ checks the design, not the code. A correct specification says nothing about whether the implementation matches it. Engineers can write code that diverges from the verified design, and the model checker will never know.

Still, catching design bugs early is enormously valuable: a flaw in a replication or recovery protocol found in a spec costs far less than one found after deployment across the fleet.

quiz.q: What can TLA+ model checking find that testing and code reviews usually miss, and what can't it check?
quiz.a: It systematically explores all interleavings of a small design, finding rare long traces like a 35-step DynamoDB bug. But it checks the design, not the actual code.

title: ShardStore: executable models check real S3 code daily
body:
ShardStore is the key-value storage node inside Amazon S3, written in Rust. The SOSP 2021 paper by Bornholt et al. describes how AWS validated its real code, not just its design.

Instead of a full proof, the team wrote executable reference models: simple versions of the system, such as a hash map, that define correct behavior. Property-based testing and model checking then compared the real implementation to the model, including under crashes and concurrency. This prevented 16 issues from reaching production.
deeper:
The prevented issues included subtle crash-consistency bugs (where recovery after a crash leaves state that does not match what was acknowledged) and concurrency bugs. These are exactly the bugs normal tests miss.

How it works in practice: property-based testing generates many random sequences of operations, applies each to both the real ShardStore and the simple reference model, and checks they give the same results. Crashes can be injected at arbitrary points, and the recovered state must still match what the model allows. Model checking explores concurrent interleavings more systematically.

A key success factor was adoption. Normal engineers, not only formal-methods experts, extended the checks as the code changed. Because the reference models were simple and executable, the checks could be maintained alongside the code, so verification kept pace with development rather than going stale.

The chapter's lesson is practical: you do not need a full proof. You need a precise, executable definition of correct, and automation that checks the real code against it every day.

quiz.q: What is an executable reference model, and why was it effective for ShardStore?
quiz.a: A simple implementation, like a hash map, defining correct behavior. Automated tests compare real code to it under crashes and concurrency, and ordinary engineers could maintain it.

title: Replication vs backup: the most important distinction
body:
This is the single most important distinction in data protection. Replication keeps copies in sync: when the primary changes, replicas change too, within milliseconds or seconds. A backup is a copy from an earlier point in time, kept separately, that does not change when the primary changes.

Replication protects against hardware failure. Backups protect against mistakes. In short: replication copies your mistakes; backups let you go back before the mistake.
deeper:
The chapter's diagram makes it concrete. A bad write or delete hits the primary at 10:00. Through sync or async replication, replica 1 is now bad and replica 2 is now bad, within seconds. Meanwhile, a backup taken at 04:00 is still good. Recovery restores to 04:00, then replays logs up to 09:59, just before the mistake.

The reason is structural. Replication's job is to make copies identical as fast as possible, which is exactly what you want when a disk dies and exactly what you do not want when the change itself is the problem. A backup's value comes from being frozen and separate: it deliberately does not follow the primary.

This leads to the chapter's key takeaway: replication copies mistakes. Only point-in-time, immutable, independently stored, and regularly restored backups protect against deletion, corruption, and ransomware. Each adjective matters: point-in-time to go before the mistake, immutable so attackers cannot destroy it, independently stored so a provider or account event cannot reach it, and regularly restored so you know it works.

quiz.q: Why can't replication substitute for backups?
quiz.a: Replication instantly copies every change, including bad writes and deletes, to all replicas. Backups are frozen earlier copies, so they let you return to before the mistake.

title: Four disasters replication copies instantly
body:
Replication does not protect against four common disasters, because it replicates each one instantly. A bug that writes bad data. A user or engineer running DELETE or rm -rf on the wrong thing. Ransomware encrypting your data. A bad schema migration.

In each case the primary receives a valid-looking change, and replication dutifully pushes it to every copy, often within seconds. Afterwards, all replicas are equally damaged, and no amount of redundancy can bring back the old data.
deeper:
These four share a trait: from the storage system's point of view, nothing failed. A bug's writes are accepted writes. A delete is an authorized operation. Ransomware using stolen credentials looks like a normal client rewriting files. A schema migration is a deliberate change. The system is working perfectly, doing the wrong thing.

This connects to the chapter's check-your-understanding question: a team replicates the messages database to three regions in active-active mode, and a product manager says they do not need backups. The reply: replication copies deletes, bugs, bad migrations, and ransomware to all three regions within seconds. You still need point-in-time backups, ideally immutable and stored in a separate account, and you must test restores.

The AWS disaster recovery whitepaper makes the same point: even active-active needs backups, because for data corruption or deletion the recovery point will always be before the disaster was discovered. The GitLab 2017 incident shows it in practice: a delete on the primary, and replication was useless because the secondary had just been wiped.

quiz.q: A PM says three-region active-active replication means no backups are needed. What do you reply?
quiz.a: Replication copies deletes, bugs, bad migrations, and ransomware to all regions within seconds. You still need point-in-time, ideally immutable, separately stored backups, and tested restores.

title: Snapshots: cheap copy-on-write, but they die with the system
body:
A snapshot is a point-in-time image of a volume, file system, or database. Most modern systems make snapshots with copy-on-write: the snapshot shares blocks with the live data, and only blocks that later change are copied. That makes snapshots fast to create and cheap to keep.

But a snapshot stored in the same system and account dies with that system or account. To make a snapshot a true backup, copy it somewhere else, outside the failure domain of the original.
deeper:
Copy-on-write is why snapshots are nearly instant: creating one just records which blocks exist at that moment. When the live data later modifies a block, the old version is preserved for the snapshot, and the new version goes elsewhere. Storage cost grows only with the amount of change, not with the size of the volume.

That sharing is also the weakness. The snapshot and the live data depend on the same underlying storage, metadata, and account. If the system has a bug that corrupts shared blocks, both are affected. If the account is compromised, deleted, or closed, the snapshots go with it. If the provider's control plane deletes the environment, as happened to UniSuper in 2024, in-environment snapshots vanish too.

So snapshots are excellent for fast recovery from small logical mistakes, like undoing a bad change an hour ago. For disaster protection, they must be copied to an independent location: another account, region, or provider. GitLab's 2017 incident also shows the operational side: Azure disk snapshots were simply not enabled for the database servers, so the feature that could have helped did not exist.

quiz.q: Why isn't a snapshot in the same account a real backup?
quiz.a: It shares storage and account with live data, so a system bug, account compromise, or provider deletion destroys both. Copying it elsewhere makes it a true backup.

title: Point-in-time recovery: full backup plus log replay
body:
Point-in-time recovery (PITR) combines a full backup with a continuous log of changes, such as a database's write-ahead log or binlog. To recover to 09:59, you restore the last full backup, then replay the log up to 09:59, just before the bad change at 10:00.

Amazon RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, and Google Cloud SQL all offer PITR, typically with a retention window of days to weeks. It gives the best recovery point for logical mistakes.
deeper:
PITR solves a gap in plain backups. With nightly backups alone, a mistake at 10:00 means restoring the 04:00 backup and losing six hours of good writes. With PITR, the log fills in everything between the backup and the moment before the mistake, so you lose almost nothing.

In the chapter's terms, PITR gives the best RPO (recovery point objective, how much data you can afford to lose) for logical mistakes like bad writes, deletes, and failed migrations.

The trade-off is restore speed. Replay means re-applying every change since the last full backup, in order. For a large, busy database, that can be a lot of log, and replay can take hours. So PITR improves RPO but can hurt RTO (recovery time objective). Teams manage this by taking full backups more frequently, which shortens the log to replay.

The retention window also matters: if a corruption is discovered after the window has passed, PITR cannot reach back far enough. Silent corruption discovered weeks later may need older backups.

quiz.q: What does PITR improve, and what is its main cost?
quiz.a: It improves RPO for logical mistakes by replaying logs to just before the error. The cost is slow restores for large datasets, since the whole log must be replayed.

title: Immutable backups: not even root can delete them
body:
Modern ransomware attacks backups first: it tries to delete or encrypt them, then the primary. So a backup must survive an attacker who has admin credentials.

Immutable backups cannot be changed or deleted until a retention date, even by an admin. Amazon S3 Object Lock in compliance mode is an example: no user, not even the account root user, can delete a locked object version before its retention date. Azure Blob immutable storage and Google Cloud Storage bucket lock offer similar features.
deeper:
The threat model here is different from hardware failure or accidental deletion. An attacker with stolen admin credentials can do anything an admin can do. If backups are protected only by permissions, the attacker simply uses those permissions to destroy them. Ransomware operators know victims with working backups do not pay, so wiping backups is a standard first step.

Immutability shifts protection from permission to policy that nobody can override. In S3 Object Lock compliance mode, the retention date is enforced by the storage service itself; even the root account cannot delete a locked object version before that date. The attacker can encrypt the live data, but the locked backup versions survive until their retention date, by which time you have restored.

The trade-off is inflexibility: you truly cannot delete locked data early, even for legitimate reasons like reducing cost or removing data written there by mistake. Retention periods must be chosen carefully.

This is why teams have extended the classic 3-2-1 backup rule with 1 immutable copy.

quiz.q: Why must a modern backup be able to survive an attacker who has admin credentials?
quiz.a: Ransomware targets backups first. If admins can delete backups, so can an attacker with stolen admin credentials; immutability enforces retention that even root cannot override.

title: Air gaps: tapes off-site, or a separate cloud account
body:
Air-gapped backups are logically or physically disconnected from production. The classic example is tapes stored off-site: no network path reaches them.

In the cloud, a logical air gap is a separate account or organization, with separate credentials, that production cannot write to or delete from. Going further, separate credentials and even separate providers protect against a provider-level mistake. The goal is simple: no single compromised credential, bug, or control-plane action can reach both production and its backups.
deeper:
Air gaps attack the same threat as immutability from a different angle. Immutability says the data cannot be deleted; an air gap says the attacker, bug, or tool cannot even reach it.

A logical air gap works because cloud permissions are scoped to accounts and organizations. If backups live in a separate account whose credentials production systems and their operators never hold, then compromising production, or a runaway script in production, does not grant access to the backups. Production can neither write to nor delete from the backup account.

Separate providers are the strongest version. A single provider's control plane can, through bug or mistake, affect every account and region you hold with them. The UniSuper case in 2024 shows it: data in two Google Cloud regions was deleted at once by a provider-side tool, and what saved them was backups held with a separate service provider.

The trade-off is operational effort: separate accounts and providers mean separate tooling, credentials management, and restore procedures, all of which must be tested.

quiz.q: How does a separate cloud account act as an air gap?
quiz.a: Production credentials cannot write to or delete from it, so a compromised production account, rogue script, or operator mistake in production cannot reach the backups.

title: 3-2-1, updated: add 1 immutable copy, 0 unverified restores
body:
A widely used rule of thumb for backups is 3-2-1: keep 3 copies of data, on 2 different media or systems, with 1 copy off-site.

Many teams now extend it: add 1 immutable copy, and 0 unverified restores. The additions reflect modern threats. The immutable copy defends against ransomware and attackers with admin rights. The zero-unverified rule means every backup has been proven restorable, because a backup nobody has tested might not work when you need it.
deeper:
Each number targets a failure mode. Three copies means one or two can fail and you still have data. Two different media or systems means one bug, firmware flaw, or product failure cannot take out every copy; different systems are different failure domains. One off-site copy means a building-level disaster, like fire, flood, or power, does not destroy everything.

The immutable copy was added because ransomware changed the game: attackers now deliberately destroy backups, and permission-based protection fails when credentials are stolen. An immutable copy, like S3 Object Lock in compliance mode, cannot be deleted even by root before its retention date.

The zero-unverified-restores rule captures the hardest-learned lesson in the chapter. Backups fail silently: tools break, formats change, credentials expire, alerts go nowhere. GitLab in 2017 (the chapter's heading: five backups, zero working) found its backup mechanisms broken when needed, because nobody had verified them; it was saved only by an ad hoc snapshot taken for another purpose. The only way to know a backup works is to restore it regularly and check the result.

quiz.q: Why did teams add '0 unverified restores' to the 3-2-1 rule?
quiz.a: Backups can fail silently through broken tools, version mismatches, or dead alerts. Only regularly restoring and checking proves a backup works, as GitLab's 2017 failure showed.

title: Common mistake: a backup you never restored is a hope
body:
A common mistake is never testing a restore. A backup you have not restored is a hope, not a backup.

Backups fail in quiet ways: the backup job errors out and the alert goes nowhere, the tool version no longer matches the database, the files are there but incomplete, or the restore takes far longer than anyone planned. None of this is visible until you actually try to restore, and the worst time to find out is during a real disaster.
deeper:
GitLab's January 2017 outage is the chapter's reference case. After a delete on the wrong database server, the team discovered pg_dump backups to S3 had been silently failing, because the tool was version 9.2 running against a 9.6 database, and the failure emails were rejected by DMARC. Nobody noticed because nobody was restoring from them.

A regular restore test catches all of these problems. It proves the backup files exist, are complete, are readable by current tools, and can be turned into a working system. It also measures how long a restore actually takes, which is essential for honest RTO planning. GitLab's eventual recovery copy took about 18 hours due to slow network storage, far longer than a plan would assume.

Good practice is to automate restores: periodically restore a backup into an isolated environment, run checks against it (row counts, checksums, application smoke tests), and alert if anything fails. It also means monitoring the monitors, because an alert that fails silently is the same as no alert.

quiz.q: Why is a regular restore test necessary even if backup jobs report success?
quiz.a: Backups fail silently: version mismatches, incomplete files, dead alerts, slow restores. Only an actual restore proves the data is usable and shows how long recovery takes.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: RPO and RTO: how much data lost, how long down
body:
Disaster recovery (DR) is the plan for when a whole site, region, or system is lost, or when data is destroyed at large scale. Two numbers define any DR plan.

RPO, the recovery point objective, is how much data, measured in time, you can afford to lose. An RPO of 5 minutes means you may lose at most the last 5 minutes of writes. RTO, the recovery time objective, is how long you can be down. An RTO of 1 hour means serving again within 1 hour.
deeper:
RPO looks backward from the disaster: how far back is the last good copy? It is determined by how often and how continuously data leaves the primary: nightly backups give an RPO of up to a day; asynchronous replication gives seconds; synchronous replication approaches zero for hardware disasters.

RTO looks forward: how long until users are served again? It depends on how much must be done after the disaster: restoring data, starting servers, warming caches, and redirecting traffic. Restoring terabytes from backup takes hours; flipping traffic to an already-running region takes minutes or less.

The central trade-off: lower RPO and RTO cost more money and more complexity. Continuous replication, standby infrastructure, and multi-region operation all add ongoing cost.

The senior staff lens frames it: RPO and RTO are business decisions expressed as engineering numbers. Ask the product owner what happens if you lose the last 10 minutes of messages. The answer drives the spend. Note also that for logical corruption, replication does not help RPO at all; only backups or PITR provide a clean recovery point.

quiz.q: What's the difference between RPO and RTO?
quiz.a: RPO is how much recent data you can lose, measured in time, set by how continuously data leaves the primary. RTO is how long you can be down before serving again.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: Backup-and-restore and pilot light: the cheap DR tiers
body:
The AWS disaster recovery whitepaper describes four standard strategies. The two cheapest:

Backup and restore: only backups exist in the DR region. RPO is typically hours and RTO hours to days, at the lowest cost.

Pilot light: data is replicated live to the DR region and core infrastructure is ready, but application servers are switched off. RPO is seconds to minutes; RTO is tens of minutes to hours, at low cost. Adding live data replication is what moves you from the first tier to the second.
deeper:
Backup and restore is simple: periodically ship backups to another region, and in a disaster, build the environment there and restore data into it. RPO is set by backup frequency. RTO is long because everything has to be provisioned and data restored, and restoring large datasets is slow.

Pilot light keeps the most time-consuming part, the data, continuously up to date in the DR region, so RPO drops to seconds or minutes. The name comes from a gas furnace's small always-on flame: the critical core is running, ready to ignite the rest. Databases are replicated and core infrastructure like networking is in place, but application servers are off, which keeps cost low.

In a disaster, pilot light still requires starting and scaling application servers before traffic can be served, which is why RTO is tens of minutes to hours.

The whitepaper's advice about control planes applies strongly here: starting servers relies on provisioning APIs, which may be degraded during a large disaster. Pre-provisioning what you can reduces that dependency.

quiz.q: What does pilot light add over backup-and-restore, and what does it still lack?
quiz.a: It adds live data replication and ready core infrastructure, cutting RPO to seconds or minutes. But application servers are off and must be started and scaled before serving.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: Warm standby and active-active: fast recovery, higher cost
body:
The two more expensive DR strategies from the AWS whitepaper:

Warm standby: a scaled-down but fully working copy runs in the DR region and can take traffic immediately. RPO is seconds to minutes; RTO is minutes; cost is medium.

Multi-site active-active: full production runs in each region, all serving real traffic. RPO and RTO are both near zero, at the highest cost. Each step up the ladder buys lower RPO and RTO with more cost and complexity.
deeper:
The chapter's progression: backup and restore, add live data replication to get pilot light, keep a small working copy running to get warm standby, serve real traffic from every region to get active-active.

The difference between pilot light and warm standby is a common interview question. Pilot light keeps data replicated and core infrastructure ready, but application servers are off and must be started and scaled before serving. Warm standby runs a smaller but fully working copy that can serve traffic immediately and only needs to scale up.
