Active-active eliminates failover as a special event: every region already serves users, so losing one means shifting its traffic to the others, which must have enough spare capacity. The costs are high: full infrastructure everywhere, plus the complexity of multi-region writes, conflict handling, and data ownership.

A key warning: active-active offers near-zero RPO for regional failure only. For corruption or deletion, it spreads the damage to every region instantly, so it still needs backups.

quiz.q: What is the difference between pilot light and warm standby?
quiz.a: Pilot light has data replicated but application servers off, needing startup and scaling. Warm standby runs a smaller fully working copy that serves traffic immediately and only scales up.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: Even active-active needs backups
body:
A key point from the AWS disaster recovery whitepaper: even multi-site active-active needs backups. Active-active protects you when a region fails, because other regions keep serving. But for data corruption or deletion, replication spreads the damage to all regions.

As the whitepaper puts it, for these events the recovery point will always be at some point before the disaster was discovered. Only a backup or point-in-time log from before the mistake provides that recovery point.
deeper:
This point is where DR strategy and data protection meet. The four DR tiers are mostly about surviving the loss of infrastructure: a region goes down, and you want to be serving again quickly with little data lost. Against that threat, active-active is the strongest option.

But the most common real disasters are logical: bad deploys writing garbage, mistaken deletes, ransomware, broken migrations. Active-active does the worst possible thing with these: it faithfully and quickly applies them everywhere. The more tightly synchronized the regions, the faster the damage spreads.

The phrase about the recovery point being before discovery matters for sizing retention. If corruption begins at 10:00 but is noticed at 15:00, you need a clean copy from before 10:00, not before 15:00. Silent corruption discovered days later needs backups that go back days.

The key takeaways sum it up: pick a DR strategy per data type from business RPO and RTO, and remember that even active-active needs backups.

quiz.q: Why does active-active multi-region deployment still require backups?
quiz.a: It protects against region loss, but replication spreads corruption and deletes to every region. Recovering from those needs a copy from before the disaster was discovered.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: Fail over with the data plane, not the control plane
body:
The second key point from the AWS DR whitepaper: fail over using the data plane, not the control plane. Control planes are the APIs that create resources, change DNS weights, or scale groups. Data planes are the running systems that serve requests.

Control planes are often less available than data planes and may be broken in the same disaster. So pre-provision what you need, and make failover a switch you flip, not a set of resources you create during the emergency.
deeper:
The logic: a disaster big enough to lose a region often stresses or breaks shared management services. Also, during a regional event, every customer tries to fail over at once, so provisioning APIs in surviving regions may be overloaded or throttled. A DR plan that begins with launching hundreds of servers depends on the least reliable path at the worst moment.

Data planes are built for continuous high availability, since they serve traffic all the time. Already-running servers, already-created databases, and health-check-based routing that responds automatically are far more dependable during a crisis.

In practice this means provisioning DR capacity ahead of time (which is part of why warm standby and active-active cost more), pre-creating resources, and designing traffic shifts that rely on existing mechanisms rather than on making new configuration changes.

The S3 2017 incident illustrates the dependency trap: the AWS Service Health Dashboard itself depended on S3 in us-east-1, so the status page shared a fate with the service it reported on. AWS afterwards moved it to multiple regions.

quiz.q: Why should failover avoid depending on control-plane APIs?
quiz.a: Control planes are often less available and may be broken or overloaded in the same disaster. Pre-provisioned resources flipped via the data plane are far more reliable.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: DR per data type: profiles and messages
body:
A 1-billion-user app should not use one DR strategy for everything; choose per data type.

Profiles are small and critical: users need them to log in. Suggested approach: active-active multi-region, plus PITR backups. Because the data is small, full copies everywhere are cheap.

Messages are write-heavy. Suggested approach: active-active or warm standby with asynchronous replication, accepting seconds of RPO. Losing a few seconds of messages on region loss is usually acceptable, and async replication avoids slowing every write.
deeper:
The reasoning combines criticality with cost. Profiles have the strictest availability need, since without them no one can log in and every other feature is unreachable, yet they are a small dataset. So the most expensive DR tier is affordable for them. PITR backups are still added because active-active will spread any bad write or delete to every region.

Messages are high volume and write-heavy. Synchronous cross-region replication would add inter-region latency to every message send. Asynchronous replication keeps writes fast, at the cost of losing the last few seconds of messages that had not yet replicated when a region fails. That is a business trade-off, which is the point of the senior staff lens: RPO and RTO are business decisions expressed as engineering numbers. Ask the product owner what happens if you lose the last 10 minutes of messages.

The answer determines whether seconds of RPO are acceptable or whether some message types, like payments, need stronger guarantees. Engineers should not guess; they should get the product owner to decide explicitly.

quiz.q: Why is active-active affordable for profiles, and why is async replication acceptable for messages?
quiz.a: Profiles are small, so full copies everywhere are cheap for critical login data. Messages are write-heavy; async avoids latency, and losing seconds on region loss is usually acceptable.

section: 10.6 Disaster recovery: RPO, RTO, and four strategies
title: DR per data type: blobs, logs, and the analytics lake
body:
The rest of the 1-billion-user app's data gets cheaper DR.

Photos and videos are huge blobs, too big to back up in the classic way. Suggested approach: cross-region replication plus versioning and delayed deletes; versioning protects against deletes.

Logs and events: replicated storage, with backup and restore for derived data, since it can often be re-derived from sources.

The analytics lake: backup and restore, plus snapshots of table metadata. Batch users can wait hours.
deeper:
Photos and videos show how the backup concept adapts at scale. Keeping a full second backup copy of petabytes of media is costly, so the design uses the storage system's own features. Versioning keeps old versions when objects are overwritten or deleted, and delayed deletes mean a delete does not physically remove data for some time. Together these give a point-in-time safety net against mistakes and malicious deletes without a separate full copy, while cross-region replication handles regional loss.

Logs and events lean on re-derivability. If derived datasets can be recomputed from source logs, then only the sources need strong protection; derived data can use cheap backup and restore.

The analytics lake has relaxed RTO because its users run batch jobs that can wait hours. Backup and restore is enough. Snapshots of table metadata matter because in a lake, the metadata defines which files form which table version; restoring it can recover a consistent table state cheaply.

The overall principle: pick the DR strategy per data type from business RPO and RTO.

quiz.q: How do versioning and delayed deletes protect photos without a classic full backup?
quiz.a: Versioning keeps old versions after overwrites or deletes, and delayed deletes postpone physical removal, giving a way back from mistakes without storing a separate full copy of petabytes.

title: An untested DR plan will fail
body:
An untested disaster recovery plan will fail when you need it. Typical reasons: hidden dependencies on the failed region, too little capacity elsewhere, cold caches, and stale runbooks that describe a system that no longer exists.

The only fix is to practice for real: deliberately take down or drain a data center or region and see what breaks. Large operators such as Google, Meta, and Netflix run exercises of this kind; Google's, for example, uncovered hidden dependencies on systems that were supposed to be down.
deeper:
Each failure reason is invisible on paper. Hidden dependencies: a service in the surviving region quietly calls an authentication or configuration service in the failed region, and everything stalls. Too little capacity: surviving regions were sized for normal load and cannot absorb the failed region's traffic. Cold caches: the surviving region's caches do not hold the failed region's hot data, so backend load spikes. Stale runbooks: steps reference renamed tools or removed systems.

These problems accumulate continuously as systems change, so a test passed last year says little about today. That is why DR testing must be regular, not one-off.

It also connects to a lesson from the S3 2017 incident: if you have never done a cold start at current scale, you do not know how long it takes. S3's index and placement subsystems needed full restarts that took far longer than expected because the system had grown.

The following cards describe how Google (DiRT), Meta (Storm and Maelstrom), and Netflix (Chaos Kong) practice, plus what storage specifically adds to region evacuation.

quiz.q: Why must DR tests be repeated regularly rather than done once?
quiz.a: Systems change constantly, creating new hidden dependencies, capacity gaps, and stale runbooks. A past test only proves the old system worked; regular tests catch new problems.

title: Google DiRT: simulate disasters, including missing people
body:
Google's DiRT (Disaster Recovery Testing) program runs large, company-wide exercises that simulate disasters, such as taking a data center offline or making key people unavailable. Kripa Krishnan described the program in ACM Queue in 2012.

The tests found problems such as hidden dependencies on systems that were supposed to be down, and processes that depended on one person. DiRT treats organizational failure, not just technical failure, as part of the disaster to rehearse.
deeper:
The inclusion of people is the distinctive part. In a real disaster, the one engineer who knows how a system works may be unreachable, asleep, or affected by the same event. Making key people unavailable during a test exposes single points of human failure: procedures only one person understands, credentials only one person holds, and approvals only one person can give.

The technical finding, hidden dependencies on systems that were supposed to be down, is the classic DR surprise. During a test, when a data center is taken offline, services that were believed to be independent turn out to call into it, and fail. Finding that during a planned exercise, with people ready to roll back, is far cheaper than finding it during a real outage.

The broader lesson is that DR readiness is a property of the whole organization: systems, runbooks, people, and communication. Company-wide exercises test the whole thing at once, which is why Google runs them at large scale rather than as isolated team drills.

quiz.q: What kinds of problems did Google's DiRT exercises uncover?
quiz.a: Hidden dependencies on systems supposed to be down, and processes relying on a single person. DiRT tests both technical and organizational single points of failure.

title: Meta's drain tests: Storm and Maelstrom
body:
Meta runs large drain tests, in which production traffic is moved away from an entire data center and later restored. Meta's disaster-readiness program, publicly called Storm, was described in talks around 2016.

The OSDI 2018 paper on Maelstrom describes the system Meta built to drain traffic safely, which understands dependencies between services. It had been in production for over four years and had helped mitigate more than 100 data center outages.
deeper:
A drain moves real production traffic, not simulated traffic, away from a data center. That is the most honest test: if the remaining data centers cannot absorb the load, or a service still depends on the drained one, it shows up with real users.

The hard part is ordering. Services depend on each other, so draining them in the wrong order can break things: pull a backend before its front ends and requests fail. Maelstrom encodes dependencies between services so it drains interdependent traffic safely and efficiently, in the right sequence, with checks along the way.

The payoff is that the same tool serves both practice and real emergencies. Because drains are routine, when a real problem hits a data center, operators use a well-exercised tool rather than an untested runbook. That is why Maelstrom had helped mitigate more than 100 data center outages in over four years in production.

This embodies the chapter's theme that failover should be a switch you flip, and that the switch only works if you flip it regularly.

quiz.q: Why is routinely draining real traffic valuable beyond just testing?
quiz.a: It proves remaining capacity and dependencies with real load, and makes the drain tool well-exercised, so the same tool reliably mitigates real outages; Maelstrom helped with over 100.

title: Netflix Chaos Kong: evacuating an entire AWS region
body:
Netflix runs on AWS in multiple regions in active-active mode. Its chaos engineering tools include Chaos Kong, which simulates the failure of an entire AWS region by evacuating traffic from it.

Netflix described Chaos Kong exercises in 2015 as a regular practice to prove that the surviving regions can absorb the load. Rather than trusting that active-active works, Netflix routinely proves it by removing a region and watching the others take over.
deeper:
Chaos engineering is the practice of deliberately injecting failures into production to find weaknesses before real failures do. Chaos Kong applies it at the largest scale Netflix operates: a whole region.

The key question an evacuation answers is capacity. In active-active mode each region handles a share of traffic. When one region is removed, its users shift to the others, which must have enough headroom for compute and for storage. Only by actually doing it can you be confident the headroom is real and that scaling, caching, and routing all behave.

The regular cadence matters for the same reason as other DR tests: systems drift. New services, new dependencies, and growing traffic can quietly erode the ability to survive a region loss.

Chaos Kong also complements the AWS whitepaper's advice. Evacuation relies on traffic routing to existing, running regions rather than on creating resources during the emergency. However, as the next card notes, storage brings its own evacuation challenges that compute does not.

quiz.q: What does a Chaos Kong exercise prove that a design review cannot?
quiz.a: That surviving regions really can absorb an entire region's traffic, with enough capacity, working routing, and no hidden dependencies, proven with real production load.

title: Evacuating a region: the three extra problems storage adds
body:
Storage adds three problems to region evacuation. First, surviving regions need enough storage IOPS and bandwidth, and storage cannot be added in minutes the way compute can. Second, writes not yet replicated out of the failed region are lost or stranded; that gap is your RPO. Third, if data is owned by one region, ownership must move to another region without two regions writing the same record at once.

Each must be planned before the evacuation, not during it.
deeper:
Capacity: compute can often scale by launching instances in minutes, but storage capacity is physical disks with data on them. The surviving regions must already hold the data and already have spare IOPS and bandwidth to serve the extra load. If they do not, evacuation causes a storage overload in the healthy regions.

Unreplicated writes: with asynchronous replication, recent writes in the failed region may not have reached any other region. They are either lost (if the region never comes back) or stranded (they exist but are inaccessible, and when the region returns, they must be reconciled with changes made elsewhere in the meantime). This is RPO made concrete.

Ownership: many systems give each record a home region that accepts its writes, to avoid conflicts. On evacuation, ownership must transfer. If the old region is merely unreachable rather than dead, and it keeps accepting writes while the new owner also does, two regions write the same record, causing split-brain conflicts or lost updates. Transferring ownership safely requires careful fencing.

quiz.q: During evacuation, why can't storage capacity simply be scaled up like compute?
quiz.a: Storage is physical disks that must already hold the data. Capacity and data can't be added in minutes, so surviving regions must be pre-provisioned with enough IOPS and bandwidth.

section: 10.8 Blast-radius reduction: cells and shuffle sharding
title: Blast radius: how many users one failure can hurt
body:
Every large outage raises the same question: why did one mistake affect so many customers? The design answer is to limit the blast radius: the set of users or data affected by one failure.

Instead of trying to prevent every failure, which is impossible, you structure the system so any single failure, whether a bug, overload, bad deploy, or poison request, can only reach a small portion of users. The main tools are cells, shuffle sharding, and staged deployments.
deeper:
The mindset shift is from prevention to containment. The incidents in this chapter show failures come from typos, bad deploys, bugs, and bad defaults, and no process eliminates all of those. What design can control is how far a failure spreads once it happens.

Blast radius applies to data and to availability. For availability, a bad deploy that crashes servers should hit a few customers, not all. For data, a buggy compaction or a destructive tool should touch a slice of the data, not the whole region.

The tools each limit a different dimension. Cells limit how much breaks: each cell is an independent stack serving a subset of customers. Shuffle sharding limits who breaks together: each customer gets a random combination of servers so one bad customer rarely takes out others entirely. Staged deployments limit when it breaks: changes reach a small group first, so problems are caught early while small.

The S3 2017 fix of partitioning the index into smaller cells, and Azure 2014's enforced flighting, both came from incidents where the blast radius was far too large.

quiz.q: What does limiting blast radius aim to achieve, if it can't prevent failures?
quiz.a: It contains each failure, whether bug, bad deploy, overload, or poison request, to a small set of users or data, instead of letting one mistake hit everyone.

section: 10.8 Blast-radius reduction: cells and shuffle sharding
title: Cells: independent copies of the whole stack
body:
A cell is a complete, independent copy of the service stack, including front ends, metadata, and storage, that serves only a subset of customers or data. A thin routing layer maps each customer to a cell.

Cells do not share state, so a bug, overload, or bad deploy in one cell affects only that cell's customers. For example, with three cells for users A to F, G to M, and N to Z, a bad deploy that hits cell 2 affects only users G to M.
deeper:
The routing layer is deliberately thin: its only job is to map a customer to a cell, so it has little logic that can fail. Everything else is duplicated per cell and isolated.

Cells also restart faster, because each one is smaller. This is why AWS sped up cell partitioning of S3's index after the 2017 outage: the index subsystem had grown so large that a full restart took far longer than expected. Smaller cells mean smaller, faster, better-understood cold starts.

Cells pair naturally with staged deployment. Deploy changes one cell at a time, with health checks between cells; Microsoft calls this flighting. If the change is bad, it breaks one cell, the checks catch it, and rollout stops before the rest are touched.

The costs: more total infrastructure and operational overhead (many stacks to run and monitor), and difficulty with operations that span cells, like a customer whose data grows beyond one cell. Moving a customer between cells also requires migration.

quiz.q: Why did AWS speed up partitioning S3's index into cells after 2017?
quiz.a: The large index subsystem took far longer than expected to restart. Smaller cells restart faster and confine a failure or bad deploy to a subset of customers.

section: 10.8 Blast-radius reduction: cells and shuffle sharding
title: Shuffle sharding: give each customer a random set of servers
body:
Plain sharding puts each customer on a fixed group of servers. If one customer sends a poison request that crashes servers, every customer on that group goes down.

Shuffle sharding instead gives each customer a random combination of servers. With 8 workers and 2 per customer, there are 28 possible pairs. A bad customer can take down only its own pair. Another customer loses both workers only if it has exactly the same pair; if only one is shared, the client retries on the other worker.
deeper:
The math is combinatorics. With plain sharding into 4 groups of 2, a poison customer kills its group and 25% of customers go down with it. With shuffle sharding, the 8 workers form 28 distinct pairs. A poison customer crashes its 2 workers. Customers who share one worker with it still have one healthy worker to retry on. Only customers with the identical pair lose both, roughly 1 in 28.

It gets dramatically better at scale. AWS Route 53 uses the pattern with 2,048 virtual name servers and 4 per customer domain, giving about 730 billion possible combinations. Two customers almost never share all their servers, so an attack or poison query against one domain essentially never fully takes down another.

The requirement is that clients must retry across their assigned servers; shuffle sharding relies on partial overlap being survivable. It also uses the same total server count as plain sharding: no extra hardware, just smarter assignment.

The senior staff lens: cells limit how much breaks; shuffle sharding limits who breaks together.

quiz.q: With 8 workers and 2 per customer, why does shuffle sharding hurt far fewer customers than fixed groups?
quiz.a: A poison customer kills only its own pair. Others sharing one worker retry on their other worker; only those with the identical pair, one of 28 combinations, fully go down.

section: 10.8 Blast-radius reduction: cells and shuffle sharding
title: Cells, shuffle sharding, staged rollout: how much, who, when
body:
Senior staff lens: the three blast-radius tools each limit a different dimension. Cells limit how much breaks, since each failure is confined to one cell's subset of customers. Shuffle sharding limits who breaks together, since customers rarely share all their servers. Staged deployments limit when it breaks: early, and small, before a bad change reaches everyone.

A mature storage service uses all three, because each covers failures the others miss.
deeper:
Why all three: they cover different failure types. Cells protect against anything that can take down a whole stack, such as a bad deploy, overload, or metadata failure; they bound the damage to one cell. Shuffle sharding protects against per-customer problems inside shared infrastructure, such as a poison request or a noisy neighbor, by making sure one customer's failure mostly lands on servers other customers only partly depend on. Staged rollouts protect against the most common trigger of all, change, by exposing each change to a small slice first and stopping on bad health signals.

They compose naturally: deploy one cell at a time (staged rollout across cells), and inside each cell assign customers to servers with shuffle sharding.

The incidents show what happens without them. Azure 2014 skipped staged rollout and a bad change hit many regions at once. S3 2017 had a huge index subsystem that was slow to restart, prompting faster cell partitioning. The chapter's key takeaway: limit blast radius with cells, shuffle sharding, staged rollouts, and guardrails on destructive tools.

quiz.q: Which blast-radius dimension does each of cells, shuffle sharding, and staged rollouts limit?
quiz.a: Cells limit how much breaks, shuffle sharding limits who breaks together, and staged rollouts limit when it breaks, catching bad changes early while their impact is small.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: S3 2017: one wrong input took down us-east-1
body:
On February 28, 2017, an Amazon S3 engineer ran a command to remove a small number of servers from a billing subsystem. One input was wrong, and a much larger set of servers was removed.

That included servers in two critical S3 subsystems: the index subsystem, holding metadata and location of every object in the region, and the placement subsystem, which chooses where new data goes. Both needed a full restart, and S3 had grown so much that the restart took far longer than expected.
deeper:
The timeline: the index subsystem started to recover at 12:26 PM PST and was fully back at 1:18 PM. Placement was fully back at 1:54 PM. During this time objects in us-east-1 could not be read, although no data was lost, making this the chapter's example of durability without availability.

The impact spread widely because many AWS services and websites depended on S3 in us-east-1. Even the AWS Service Health Dashboard depended on it, so the page meant to report the outage was itself affected.

The key amplifier was the restart. S3 had grown so much that a full restart of these subsystems took far longer than expected. The chapter's lesson: if you have never done a cold start at current scale, you do not know how long it takes.

In the patterns table: root trigger, wrong command input; what turned it into a disaster, no guardrail, a huge subsystem, and slow cold start; design fix, safe tools and cells.

quiz.q: In the S3 2017 outage, what turned a mistyped command into a multi-hour regional outage?
quiz.a: The tool had no guardrail, so it removed far too many servers, and the huge index and placement subsystems needed full restarts that took far longer than expected at current scale.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: S3 2017 lesson: guardrails on tools, restartable systems
body:
After the 2017 S3 outage, AWS fixed the capacity-removal tool to remove capacity slowly and never below a minimum, and added similar safety checks to other tools. It sped up splitting the index into smaller cells, and moved the Service Health Dashboard to multiple regions.

The lesson: tools must have guardrails, and large systems must be restartable. If you have never done a cold start at current scale, you do not know how long it takes.
deeper:
Each fix maps to one amplifier. Removing capacity slowly and never below a minimum means a typo can no longer remove a huge set of servers at once; the tool refuses to go below what the system needs. Applying the same checks to other tools recognizes that the problem was the class of tool, not one command.

Cell partitioning addresses restart time: smaller index cells restart faster and independently, and a failure in one does not require restarting the whole region's index.

Moving the dashboard to multiple regions removes a dependency where the status page shared a fate with the service it was reporting on.

The restartability lesson generalizes. Systems that run continuously for years accumulate state and scale, and their cold-start behavior drifts unmeasured. The only way to know is to practice restarts, which links to the DR testing in Section 10.7.

The chapter's senior staff lens on destructive operations asks exactly the questions S3's tool lacked: is there a limit, such as never removing more than X at once?

quiz.q: Why did AWS change the capacity tool to never remove capacity below a minimum?
quiz.a: So a mistyped input can't remove far more servers than the system needs to function. The tool itself enforces safety instead of relying on correct human input.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: GitLab 2017: five backups, zero working
body:
On January 31, 2017, during an incident with database replication, a tired GitLab engineer ran a delete on what he thought was the secondary database server. It was the primary. About 300 GB of data was removed before he stopped it.

Then the team found every safety net broken: pg_dump backups to S3 had silently failed, Azure disk snapshots were not enabled for the database servers, and replication was useless because the secondary had just been wiped.
deeper:
The pg_dump failure had two layers. The backups used 9.2 tools against a 9.6 database, so they did not work. The failure notification emails were rejected by DMARC, an email authentication policy, so nobody received them. The backups had been failing silently for some time.

The replication point is the replication-versus-backup lesson in action. Replication is a hot copy of the current state. With the secondary just wiped as part of the replication incident and the primary deleted, there was no good copy left in the replication system at all.

In the patterns table: root trigger, delete on wrong server; what turned it into a disaster, backups never tested and alerts silently failing; design fix, restore testing and monitoring the monitors.

The human element is worth noting: the engineer was tired and working during an ongoing replication incident, and believed he was on the secondary. The chapter's senior staff lens on destructive operations would ask: was there a delay, a confirmation by a second person or system, or a copy outside the blast radius?

quiz.q: Why didn't replication help GitLab recover from the 2017 delete?
quiz.a: The secondary had just been wiped during the replication incident, and replication only mirrors current state. With the primary deleted, no good copy existed anywhere in the replication system.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: GitLab's rescue: a 6-hour-old snapshot taken by accident
body:
GitLab recovered from a manual LVM snapshot that happened to be taken about six hours earlier for another purpose. Copying it took about 18 hours because of slow network storage.

About 5,000 projects, 5,000 comments, and 700 new user accounts from the six-hour window were lost. Git repositories and wikis were not affected. GitLab live-streamed the recovery and published a detailed, honest postmortem.

Lesson: backups must be monitored and restored regularly. An alert that fails silently is the same as no alert.
deeper:
The recovery was luck, not design. The snapshot that saved GitLab existed only because someone had made it for an unrelated reason. Without it, the loss would have been far greater. The effective RPO was about six hours, and the RTO was at least the 18-hour copy, numbers no one had planned for because no restore had ever been rehearsed.

The 18-hour copy shows why restore testing must measure time, not just correctness. Knowing a backup exists tells you nothing about how long it takes to get data back. Slow network storage turned a recovery into most of a day of downtime.

The honesty of the response became a model for the industry. Live-streaming the recovery and publishing a candid postmortem, including every failed safety net, turned an embarrassing incident into widely used teaching material.

The core lesson has two parts. Backups must be restored regularly, because that is the only way to know they work. And monitoring must itself be monitored: the pg_dump failure alerts were being rejected by DMARC, so the alerting system failed silently, which is the same as having no alert.

quiz.q: What does 'monitor the monitors' mean in the GitLab 2017 context?
quiz.a: Backup failure alerts were rejected by DMARC and never arrived. You must verify alerts actually reach people, because a silently failing alert is the same as no alert.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: Azure 2014: skipping the staged rollout
body:
In November 2014, a performance change for Azure Table storage was deployed. It was wrongly enabled for Azure Blob storage front ends too, and it exposed a bug that put them into an infinite loop.

Worse, engineers skipped the normal flighting process, deploying to small batches first, because the change had already been tested. It went to many regions at once. The interruption lasted hours and also broke Virtual Machines whose disks lived in Blob storage.
deeper:
Two mistakes compounded. First, a configuration error: a change meant for Table storage was applied to Blob storage, a different service, where it triggered an infinite loop bug. Second, a process bypass: because the change had already been tested, the team felt confident enough to skip flighting and push it broadly. Prior testing did not catch the bug that surfaced once the change reached Blob storage front ends, which is exactly what small first batches exist to catch.

The dependency chain amplified the damage: Virtual Machines used Blob storage for their disks, so a storage front-end failure became a compute outage too.

Microsoft's key fix was to make the deployment tooling enforce incremental rollout, rather than relying on humans to follow policy.

Lesson: policies that depend on humans will eventually be skipped. Encode them in tools. In the patterns table: root trigger, config applied to wrong service; what turned it into a disaster, skipped staged rollout; design fix, tooling enforces flighting.

quiz.q: What was Microsoft's key fix after the 2014 Azure Storage outage, and why that approach?
quiz.a: Deployment tooling now enforces incremental rollout. Policies that rely on humans eventually get skipped under confidence or pressure, so the tools must make the safe path mandatory.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: DynamoDB 2015: a network blip became a metadata storm
body:
On September 20, 2015, a short network disruption made many DynamoDB storage servers ask the internal metadata service for their partition membership at the same time. Growth in Global Secondary Indexes had made these responses much larger.

The metadata service overloaded, storage servers could not renew their membership, and they took themselves offline. Error rates in us-east-1 peaked around 55%, and SQS, Auto Scaling, and CloudWatch were affected. Fixes included more capacity and splitting the metadata service into independent instances.
deeper:
The failure was a feedback loop. Storage servers must periodically confirm their partition membership with the metadata service. The brief network disruption caused many to re-request membership at once. Because Global Secondary Indexes had grown, each response was much larger than before, so the metadata service was doing far more work per request. It could not keep up, requests timed out, storage servers failed to renew, took themselves offline, and retried, adding more load.

The system had been fine in steady state; the vulnerability only showed when many servers acted in sync. Growth had silently eroded the margin.

The fixes address both parts: more capacity for headroom, and splitting the metadata service into independent instances, so the load and any failure are divided, a form of cells for metadata.

Lesson: metadata is often the real bottleneck, and synchronized retries turn a blip into an outage. In the patterns table: root trigger, network blip; what turned it into a disaster, metadata overload and synchronized retries; design fix, capacity and split metadata.

quiz.q: How did a short network blip turn into a major DynamoDB outage in 2015?
quiz.a: Many storage servers simultaneously re-requested now-larger membership data, overloading the metadata service; failed renewals took servers offline and retries added load, a synchronized feedback loop.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: UniSuper 2024: a blank field deleted a whole private cloud
body:
UniSuper, a large Australian pension (superannuation) fund, ran on Google Cloud VMware Engine (GCVE). In May 2024 its entire private cloud subscription was deleted, and members could not access their accounts for well over a week.

Google's explanation: during the initial deployment in 2023, Google operators used an internal tool and left one input parameter blank. The system applied an unexpected default, a fixed one-year term. When the year ended, the system automatically deleted the private cloud, with no customer notification.
deeper:
Why no notification: the deletion was not customer-initiated, so the normal flows that warn customers about deletions did not apply. From the system's point of view, a subscription term simply expired and cleanup ran as designed.

The chain is striking for how ordinary each step was: an internal tool, a blank field, a default value, a scheduled expiry, an automated cleanup. No single step looked dangerous. The danger was a default that silently set an expiry nobody intended, a year before it acted.

Google's remediation: it deprecated the manual tool, reviewed all GCVE deployments, and fixed the auto-deletion behavior.

In the patterns table: root trigger, blank parameter and bad default; what turned it into a disaster, auto-delete across all regions; design fix, independent backups and safe defaults.

The senior staff lens on destructive operations applies directly: was there a delay like a soft delete, a notification to the owner, a second system confirming? Any two would likely have kept this small.

quiz.q: What made the UniSuper deletion possible without anyone noticing in advance?
quiz.a: A blank parameter triggered a default one-year term, and at expiry the system auto-deleted the private cloud. Since it wasn't customer-initiated, no notification was sent.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: UniSuper lesson: multi-region isn't independence
body:
UniSuper had copies in two geographic regions within Google Cloud, but the provider-side deletion removed both. Recovery was possible because UniSuper also kept backups with a separate service provider, which the joint statement said minimised data loss and made restoration possible.

Lesson: multi-region is not independence if one control plane, one account, or one contract can delete every region at once. For critical data, keep at least one copy outside the blast radius of your primary provider's control plane.
deeper:
This is the failure domain idea applied beyond hardware. Two regions protect against a regional disaster like a power loss, flood, or network cut. They do not protect against anything that acts on both regions through a shared layer. Here the shared layer was the provider's control plane and the subscription: one deletion action applied to the whole private cloud, wherever it ran.

The backups at a separate provider worked because they were outside that blast radius entirely. Google's tools, accounts, and contracts had no reach over them. This is the strongest form of the air gap described in Section 10.5: separate credentials and separate providers protect against provider-level mistakes.

This is also the answer to the chapter's check-your-understanding question: both regions shared one provider, account, and control plane, so one deletion removed both; backups at a separate provider saved them.

For the 1-billion-user app, it means the most critical data, like profiles and metadata, should have a copy that no single provider, account, or contract can delete.

quiz.q: UniSuper had data in two regions. Why didn't that protect it, and what did?
quiz.a: Both regions shared one provider, account, and control plane, so one deletion removed both. Backups held with a separate service provider made restoration possible.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: No incident was 'too many disks failed at random'
body:
Across the chapter's incidents, the triggers were a wrong command input (S3 2017), a delete on the wrong server (GitLab 2017), a config applied to the wrong service (Azure 2014), a network blip (DynamoDB 2015), a blank parameter with a bad default (UniSuper 2024), and lightning (Google 2015).

The amplifiers were missing guardrails, untested backups, skipped staged rollouts, metadata overload, auto-delete across regions, and volatile caches. Notice that no incident was too many disks failing at random.
deeper:
The patterns table pairs each incident with its design fix. S3 2017: safe tools and cells. GitLab 2017: restore testing and monitoring the monitors. Azure 2014: tooling enforces flighting. DynamoDB 2015: capacity and split metadata. UniSuper 2024: independent backups and safe defaults. Google 2015: persistent write path.

The structure in every case is a small trigger plus a design weakness that turned it into a disaster. The triggers are mundane and unavoidable: humans mistype, networks blip, lightning strikes. What differs between a minor incident and a disaster is whether guardrails, isolation, and independent copies were in place.

This ties back to the chapter's opening claim: disks dying is the easy problem. The durability math of Section 10.2, with its nines, handles random disk failures well. Real losses and outages come from operator error, software and configuration mistakes, correlated physical events, and shared control planes, none of which appear in a nines calculation. That is why the Senior staff lens on N nines insists on asking what is outside the model.

quiz.q: What does the observation that no incident was random disk failure imply for where to invest?
quiz.a: Disk failure is handled by redundancy and repair. Invest in guardrails on tools, staged rollouts, tested independent backups, metadata capacity, and blast-radius isolation, where real incidents originate.

section: 10.9 Real incidents and what they teach
title: Five questions before any destructive operation
body:
Senior staff lens: for any destructive operation, such as deleting a bucket, removing capacity, dropping a table, or expiring a subscription, ask five questions. Is there a delay, like a soft delete or tombstone kept for days? Is there a limit, such as never removing more than X at once? Is there a second person or system that confirms? Is there a notification to the owner? Is there a copy outside the blast radius?

Most of the chapter's incidents would have been small with any two of these.
deeper:
Map the questions to the incidents. S3 2017 lacked a limit: the tool removed far more servers than intended. GitLab 2017 lacked confirmation and a verified copy: a delete ran on the primary, and the backups did not work. UniSuper 2024 lacked a delay and a notification: the private cloud was deleted automatically, with no customer warning, but it had the one saving grace of a copy outside the blast radius at a separate provider, which is why it was recoverable at all.

Each control is cheap relative to the disasters it prevents. A delay turns an irreversible action into a reversible one for a window of time. A limit caps how much damage one command can do. Confirmation catches the tired-engineer case. Notification gives the owner a chance to object. An independent copy is the last line when all else fails.

The point about any two is about layering: no single control is perfect, but two independent ones rarely fail together. This echoes Azure's lesson: build these checks into tools rather than relying on people.

quiz.q: Why does the chapter suggest any two of these five safeguards would have kept most incidents small?
quiz.a: Each safeguard catches different failures; two independent ones rarely fail together. A delay or limit plus a confirmation or independent copy turns catastrophe into a recoverable event.

title: Chapter 10 in one card: how data really gets lost
body: Durability (data not lost) and availability (reachable now) are different goals; ask for both. Drives fail at about 1 to 2% per year, so repair must be automatic. Loss needs overlapping failures in the repair window, and with three copies risk scales with repair time squared, so fast declustered repair is the cheapest win. 11 nines covers hardware, not deletes, bugs, or account events. Silent corruption, even from CPUs, needs end-to-end checksums and scrubbing. Replication copies mistakes; only real backups undo them.
deeper:
The remaining takeaways cover software, DR, and blast radius. Software bugs break every independence assumption, so AWS uses TLA+ to check designs and lightweight formal methods, as in ShardStore, to check real code against executable models.

Only point-in-time, immutable, independently stored, and regularly restored backups protect against deletion, corruption, and ransomware. Each property blocks a failure: point-in-time goes back before the mistake, immutable resists attackers with admin rights, independent storage survives account and provider events like UniSuper, and regular restores catch silent backup failures like GitLab's.

Pick a DR strategy, from backup and restore through pilot light and warm standby to active-active, per data type based on business RPO and RTO. Even active-active needs backups, and failover should use the data plane, not the control plane.

Limit blast radius with cells, shuffle sharding, staged rollouts, and guardrails on destructive tools. And remember the chapter's empirical finding: none of the major incidents studied was caused by too many disks failing at random. The hard problems are corruption, bugs, and humans or tools deleting the wrong thing.

quiz.q: Which four properties must backups have to protect against deletion, corruption, and ransomware?
quiz.a: Point-in-time, immutable, independently stored, and regularly restored: go back before the mistake, resist attackers, survive account or provider events, and be proven to work.
